Nicanor gave orders for his bodyguards to kidnap Judas. So Nicanor went with them to the camp, where Nicanor greeted him like a friend.
But Judas found out what Nicanor had in mind, and he was frightened and refused to meet with him.
When Nicanor realized that he could not trick Judas, he attacked him near the town of Caphar-Salama.
Nicanor lost about 500 soldiers in the battle, before the rest of his army retreated to the fortress in Jerusalem.

Sometime later, Nicanor went up to Mount Zion, where he was met by some priests and leaders outside the temple. They welcomed him peacefully and showed him how they offered sacrifices as a way of asking God to bless King Demetrius.
Nicanor laughed and made fun of the priests and leaders. He even spit on them and made them unfit to serve God. He was so arrogant
and angry that he said, “If Judas and his soldiers aren't handed over to me immediately, I'll return here and destroy your temple just as soon as I defeat him.” Nicanor was furious when he left.
The priests returned to the temple courtyard, where they stared at the temple and the altar. Then with tears in their eyes, they prayed:
“You have chosen this temple
Defeat Nicanor and his army!
Nicanor led his troops out of Jerusalem, and they camped near the town of Beth-Horon, where they were joined by a force of Syrian soldiers.
After Judas and his army of 3,000 soldiers set up camp near the town of Adasa, Judas prayed:
Our God, a long time ago the king of Assyria sent messengers to insult you. But your angel slaughtered 185,000 of his soldiers.
Destroy Nicanor's army today, and it will show our enemies that Nicanor cannot get away with disgracing your temple.
The battle took place on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and Nicanor's army was wiped out. He himself was the first to be killed,
and when his troops saw what had happened, they threw down their weapons and ran for their lives.
For the rest of the day, Judas and his soldiers chased the enemy troops from Adasa as far as Gazara. They blew trumpets as they went along,
and their friends rushed out from nearby villages of Judea. They attacked the enemy from the side and forced them to turn back toward Judas and his army. Not one of Nicanor's troops survived.

The Jews took everything of value from the dead enemy soldiers. Then they chopped off Nicanor's head and the right hand he had used to disgrace the temple and took them to Jerusalem, where they displayed them outside the city.
And so, there was peace in Judea for a while.
This is what Judas heard about the Romans:
Powerful Roman armies have already won great victories in Gaul. Not only have they defeated that country, but they have forced it to pay taxes.
The Romans have also captured the gold and silver mines in Spain.
In fact, by patient and careful planning, they have conquered all of Spain, even though it is a great distance from Rome.
The Roman armies have also destroyed other enemies, including kings Perseus and Philip of Macedonia
and King Antiochus the Great of Asia.
They took him alive and ordered him and his descendants to give them a lot of money and many hostages. Antiochus also had to hand over to them
the countries of India, Media, and Lydia, as well as some of the best areas he controlled. Then the Romans gave all this territory to King Eumenes.
The Romans destroyed the rest of the kingdoms and islands that opposed them, and they put Roman rulers in charge.
its rulers don't show off by wearing crowns or purple robes.
Instead, they have built a meeting house where 320 senators meet each day to pass good laws for ruling their nation.
Every year, the Romans elect one man to govern them and the countries under their control. Everyone obeys this ruler, and no one is ever jealous of him.
After making the long trip to Rome, they met with the Roman senators and said,
“Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, together with all our people, have sent us, because they want you to make a peace treaty with us Jews and let us be your allies.”
The Romans liked what Eupolemus and Jason said,
and they replied by writing a letter on sheets of bronze. They sent the letter to Jerusalem, to serve as a reminder that Rome was a friend and ally. The letter said:
We pray that all will go well with the Romans and Jews, both on land and sea, and that we will never have any wars or enemies.
As it was decided in Rome, you must not send food, weapons, money, or ships to these enemies. So keep your part of this agreement and don't expect anything in return.
In this same way, we Romans will gladly do all we can if you are attacked.
We won't supply your enemies with food, weapons, money, or ships, and we will keep our word, without any tricks.
This is the agreement that we Romans have now made with you Jews,
but it can be changed, if later we both agree to do so. And any changes will be just as binding.
The Romans also told the Jewish messengers:
If we hear of any more trouble, we will defend their rights and attack you with our army and navy.”
King Demetrius found out that Nicanor and all his soldiers had been killed. So he sent Bacchides and Alcimus the high priest back to Judea with half of his army.
On the way to Gilgal in Judea, Bacchides and Alcimus captured the town of Mesaloth in Arbela, and they killed many of the people.
They reached Jerusalem early in the year 152 of the Syrian Kingdom and set up camp outside the city.
Then they stationed 20,000 soldiers and 2,000 cavalry in the town of Berea.
Three thousand of the Jews' best soldiers were camped at Elasa under the command of Judas.
But when they saw the size of the enemy army, they were terrified and ran. Only about 800 soldiers stayed in camp.
When the fighting was about to start, Judas suddenly realized that most of his troops had deserted, and he was terribly discouraged because there was no time to bring them back.
Judas felt like giving up, but he said to his remaining troops, “Get ready to attack! We've got a good chance to win.”
But they argued with Judas and said, “We will all be killed if we attack with such a small force. Let's wait and come back with a larger army.”
Judas answered, “We will never back down from a fight with the enemy! If it's our time to die for the honor of our nation, then let's die like heroes.”
The fighting lasted from daylight until dark, and the ground trembled because of the noise.
At one point in the battle, Judas looked over at the right side of the enemy army and saw Bacchides and many of his best soldiers there. So Judas and his bravest troops attacked
and destroyed most of that part of the enemy army. The few who escaped were chased as far as Mount Azotus.
When the soldiers on the left side of Bacchides' army learned that the rest of their army had been wiped out, they swung around and attacked from behind.
The fighting was fierce, and many from both armies were either killed or wounded.
Judas himself died in the battle, and the rest of the Jews ran away.
Jonathan and Simon took the body of their brother Judas back to Modein and buried him in the family tomb.
They cried bitterly, and everyone in Israel mourned for a long time. They said:
“Judas was a mighty warrior
Indeed, Judas was a brave warrior and a great hero, and he did many other important things that are not included in this book.
After the death of Judas, some troublemakers and their worthless friends showed up again everywhere in Judea.
The crops had failed that year, and everyone in the whole country joined these troublemakers.
Bacchides appointed some godless people to rule the country,
and they searched carefully for any followers of Judas. Then they brought them to Bacchides, who laughed as he punished them.
The troubles in Israel were worse now than they had been since the time God had stopped sending prophets.
The followers of Judas got together and said to Jonathan:
Ever since your brother Judas died, we haven't had anyone like him to lead us into battle against enemies like Bacchides or against our own people who hate us.
So today we have chosen you to take the place of Judas. Be our ruler and lead us in battle.
Jonathan agreed.
Bacchides plotted to kill Jonathan as soon as he found out that Jonathan was the new leader.
But his plan failed, because Jonathan and his brother Simon were warned and escaped with their followers to a camp near the water hole at Asphar in the desert around Tekoa.
On a Sabbath, Bacchides learned where the camp was, and he led his army across the Jordan River.
Jonathan's brother John was also one of the Jewish leaders. One day, on orders from Jonathan, he asked some friendly Nabateans to guard their huge stock of supplies.
But some people of the Jambri tribe from Medeba captured John and the supplies, then rode away.
Later, Jonathan and his brother Simon were told:
Meanwhile, Jonathan and Simon had learned that this tribe had murdered their brother John. So they left camp and set an ambush on a hillside overlooking the road.

Soon they saw a noisy group of travelers with a lot of baggage. It was the bride, with her family and friends. The groom and his friends were coming to meet them, playing drums and musical instruments, and all of them were armed.
The Jews attacked from their hiding places, killing and wounding many in the wedding party. Then they took everything of value from the dead, and the others ran off into the hills.
A wedding was turned
After Jonathan and Simon had punished the tribe of Jambri, they returned to their camp in the marshes along the Jordan River.
But Bacchides found out where they were camped, and on the Sabbath he led a large army to the edge of the river.
Jonathan warned his soldiers:
and there is no way out. The enemy army is both in front of us and behind us, and the river is on one side, and the marshes covered with thornbushes are on the other.
So pray for God to rescue us.
As soon as the battle began, Jonathan tried to kill Bacchides; however, he escaped to the rear of his army.
Jonathan and his soldiers then jumped into the river and started swimming toward the other side, but the enemy troops did not go after them.
That day Bacchides lost about 1,000 men.

Bacchides returned to Jerusalem and started building high walls and strong gates for some of the towns of Judea, including Emmaus, Beth-Horon, Bethel, Timnath, Pharathon, and Tephon, and the fortress at Jericho.
He stationed soldiers in these towns, and they caused trouble for the Jews.
Bacchides also strengthened the fortress in Jerusalem and the towns of Beth-Zur and Gazara. He put soldiers and food supplies in these strongholds.
Then he took the sons of the Jewish leaders as hostages and locked them up in the Jerusalem fortress.

In the second month of the year 153 of the Syrian Kingdom, Alcimus the high priest ordered his followers to destroy the wall in the temple courtyard that prophets of earlier times had said should be built.
But no sooner had the work begun, than Alcimus got sick and everything stopped. He couldn't move or even give instructions for making out his will.
He died a very painful death.
After Bacchides learned that Alcimus had died, he returned to King Demetrius, and Judea had peace for two years.

Once again the troublemakers started plotting against Jonathan and his followers by saying, “They feel safe and aren't suspecting a thing, so let's send for Bacchides. He could easily capture them in one night.”
The troublemakers met with Bacchides and planned an attack.
Then Bacchides set out for Judea with a large army. On the way, he sent secret orders for his followers there to capture Jonathan and his troops.
and so they arrested about fifty leaders of the plot and put them to death.
Jonathan and Simon led their forces to the desert town of Beth-Basi. Part of the town had been destroyed, but they repaired it and built high walls with strong gates.
When Bacchides found out about this, he got together his whole army and sent orders to his followers in Judea.
Then he led his army to Beth-Basi and surrounded the town. His soldiers set up weapons to break through the walls, and they attacked that town for a long time.
At one point in the battle, Jonathan put his brother Simon in command of the town. Then he led a small group into the country,
where he defeated Odomera and his tribe. He also wiped out another tribe called the Phasirites.
Those who were left joined his army and helped him fight against Bacchides.
In fact, they destroyed the entire army of Bacchides and ruined all of his plans for war.
Bacchides was so furious at the troublemakers who had told him to invade Judea that he put many of them to death. Then he got ready to return to his own country.
When Jonathan found out Bacchides was about to leave Judea, he sent him some messengers who said, “Let's make peace and set our prisoners free.”
Now there was peace in Israel. Jonathan ruled from the town of Michmash and started destroying godless people everywhere in the nation.

Alexander Epiphanes was the son of King Antiochus the Fourth. He landed on the Phoenician coast and captured the city of Ptolemais in the year 160 of the Syrian Kingdom. The people welcomed Alexander as their king.
When King Demetrius found out that Alexander was in Ptolemais, he got together a mighty army and set out to attack him.
Demetrius sent Jonathan a friendly letter that flattered him.
In the letter Demetrius said:
Jonathan took this letter to Jerusalem and read it to everyone, including those in the fortress.
His enemies were terrified by the letter, because it allowed him to build up an army.
The soldiers in the fortress immediately released the hostages to Jonathan, and he let them go home to their parents.
Jonathan moved to Jerusalem and began repairing and rebuilding the city.
He ordered the workers to cut square blocks of stone and to build strong walls around Jerusalem and Mount Zion. The workers followed his orders.
Only a few Jews who were unfaithful to the Law stayed in Beth-Zur for their own safety.

Someone told King Alexander, “Jonathan and his brothers are brave fighters who have fought many wars and who know what it means to suffer. And Demetrius has promised them many things if they will join him.”
Alexander replied, “I'd better make Jonathan my friend and ally. I'll never find anyone else like him.”
Alexander then sent Jonathan a letter, in which he said:
King Alexander sends greetings to his dear friend Jonathan!
I've been told that you are a powerful soldier and the kind of man who deserves to be one of my trusted friends.
So I appoint you high priest for your nation and a friend of the king. This means that you must be a very loyal follower. I'm also sending you a purple robe and a gold crown.
During the Festival of Shelters, in the seventh month of the year 160 of the Syrian Kingdom, Jonathan became high priest; he also built up a strong army.
When King Demetrius heard the news about Alexander and Jonathan, he was deeply distressed and said,
“What have we done? Alexander's agreement with the Jews has made him very powerful.
Now I must write a friendly letter to the Jews and promise them better gifts and more honors. Then they'll come over to my side.”
And so, Demetrius wrote:
I was very pleased to learn that you have kept your promises. This means you are still my friends and allies.
If you remain loyal to me, I will reward you for everything you do.
I will give you valuable gifts and not make you pay heavy taxes.
My Jewish friends, you are excused from paying taxes on salt, as well as the other usual taxes, including the special royal tax.
And from now on, you no longer have to give me a share of your grain and fruit.
And I consider Jerusalem and the land that belongs to it so holy that I won't tax the money you receive from these places.
The high priest will take over from me the control of the Jerusalem fortress, and his own soldiers can guard it.
I will free every Jew who has been taken prisoner anywhere in my kingdom. You won't have to pay anything for them, and they won't have to pay taxes, not even on their livestock.

On special days such as festivals, Sabbaths, or the first day of a month, my officials will not collect taxes or fees from any Jew in the kingdom. And on the three days before and after festivals, my officials will not collect taxes or fees.
No one will collect taxes from you or bother you for any reason on those special days.
I will let as many as 30,000 Jewish soldiers join my army, and they will be paid the same as the other soldiers.

Some of them will help guard my main fortresses, and others will be given important jobs in the kingdom. I'll let them live by their own laws and choose their own leaders and officers. In fact, this is how things already are in Judea.
The three districts of Judea that belonged to Samaria will become a permanent part of Judea. The high priest will be the only ruler for Judea and these three districts, and everyone must obey him.
I have given the city of Ptolemais and the land around it as a gift to the temple in Jerusalem, in order to supply money to help pay for running the temple.
Every year, I'll send you 15,000 pieces of silver from the treasuries in places under my control.
For the past few years my officials have failed to send you the extra money that they should have sent. Now they will start sending it again to meet the needs of the temple.
In the past, you had to pay me 5,000 pieces of silver every year as a tax on the money the temple earned. Now this tax money will go to the priests who serve in the temple.
If anyone is hiding in or around the Jerusalem temple because they owe money to me or someone else, they are free to leave. And any property they own in my kingdom will be returned to them.
Jonathan and the others remembered how cruel King Demetrius had been to them, and they did not believe a word he had written.
Instead, they sided with King Alexander, because he had come with the best offer of peace, and they remained his allies until he died.
Alexander built up a mighty army and led it into battle against the army of Demetrius.
King Alexander sent a message to King Ptolemy the Sixth of Egypt. It said:
I've returned to rule the kingdom of my ancestors. But before I could take control, I had to do away with Demetrius.
So I destroyed him and his army, and now I am king.
Ptolemy, I would like for us to become allies. Let me marry your daughter and be your son-in-law. Then I will give each of you gifts that are worthy of a king and his daughter.
Ptolemy wrote back:
I'll let you marry my daughter, just as you asked in your letter. But first, meet me in the city of Ptolemais, so we can get to know each other.
In the year 162 of the Syrian Kingdom, Ptolemy and his daughter Cleopatra left Egypt and went to the city of Ptolemais.
The two kings met each other, and Ptolemy let Alexander marry Cleopatra. They had a very fancy wedding, just as kings always do.
Meanwhile, Jonathan the high priest received a letter from Alexander, inviting him to come to Ptolemais for a visit with him and Ptolemy.
Jonathan accepted the invitation and won their friendship by giving both kings and their trusted friends some silver and gold, as well as many other gifts.
One day, a group of troublemakers and rebels came from Judea and brought charges against Jonathan. But Alexander would not listen to them.
Instead, he let Jonathan wear the purple robes of royalty
and sit next to him. The king told his officers, “Take Jonathan to the center of the city and order everyone to stop bothering him with all these charges.”

The troublemakers listened to the officers telling everyone to leave Jonathan alone. And when they saw Jonathan standing there in his purple robes, they realized how important he was. So they all ran away.
Alexander gave Jonathan even more honors. He included him among his most trusted friends and made him governor of Judea and a general in the Syrian army.
After this, Jonathan returned to Jerusalem, safe and sound.
Demetrius the Second was the son of Demetrius, and in the year 165 of the Syrian Kingdom, he sailed from Crete to the land of his ancestors.
When Alexander heard about this, he became worried and returned to the city of Antioch.

Demetrius appointed Apollonius ruler of Southwest Syria Province. So Apollonius built up a large army and set up camp near the town of Jamnia. Then he sent the following letter to Jonathan the high priest:
Jonathan, you are the only one who is still fighting against us, and you are making others laugh and sneer at me. Why do you keep rebelling against us there in the hill country?
If you're so proud of your army, come down out of the hills and fight. You will find out that the people in the towns are on our side.
Just ask anyone, and they will tell you who I am and who my followers are. You don't stand a chance against us.
What makes you think you can win a battle in the valley against my army and cavalry? There are no rocks or stones to crawl behind, and there is no place where you can run away.
Jonathan was furious when he read this letter. He chose 10,000 soldiers, then left Jerusalem to meet his brother Simon, who was coming to help him.
The two brothers surrounded the town of Joppa, because Apollonius had soldiers there. No one would let them in at first.
But they attacked and frightened the people into opening the gates; then they took command of the town.

When Apollonius found out that they had taken Joppa, he brought 3,000 cavalry and a large force of soldiers to the town of Azotus. He wanted the Jews to think he was only passing through the town. So he led his troops out to the nearby valley, where he was sure his cavalry could protect the soldiers.
Jonathan followed Apollonius to Azotus, and a battle broke out
when 1,000 of Apollonius' cavalry suddenly left their hiding places and attacked from behind.
The cavalry surrounded Jonathan's troops and shot arrows at them from early morning until late afternoon.
But Jonathan's forces held their ground, and he told them to keep fighting until the enemy cavalry wore themselves out.
Then Simon led some of his soldiers into the battle and overpowered the enemy army. The enemy foot soldiers ran for their lives,
and the cavalry scattered over the valleys.
But Jonathan destroyed Azotus and the nearby towns and took everything of value. Then he burned down the temple with everyone inside.
Eight thousand enemy soldiers died in the battle and the fire.
Jonathan left Azotus and ordered his army to set up camp near the town of Askalon, where the people came out to honor him.
Then Jonathan and his soldiers, loaded down with everything they had taken, returned to Jerusalem.
When Alexander heard about Jonathan's victories, he gave him even more honors.
He sent a gold buckle that only the most respected members of the king's family were allowed to wear. Alexander also gave Jonathan the town of Ekron and the land around it.
King Ptolemy the Sixth of Egypt got together more ships and soldiers than anyone could count. Then he made a secret plan to take over the kingdom of his son-in-law Alexander.
Ptolemy led his forces toward Syria and told each town he came to that he was on a friendly visit. Everyone believed Ptolemy and welcomed him, just as his son-in-law Alexander had ordered them to do.
But he stationed soldiers in their towns.

The people of Azotus met Ptolemy and showed him all that was left of their town, of the nearby villages, and of the temple of Dagon that had been destroyed by fire. They also showed him the piles of dead and burned bodies they had heaped up beside the road after the battle with Jonathan.
Everyone blamed Jonathan for all the damage, but Ptolemy said nothing.
Jonathan met Ptolemy at the town of Joppa, and Jonathan honored him. The two men spent the night there,
then the next day Jonathan rode with him to the Eleutherus River before heading back for Jerusalem.
Soon Ptolemy had command of the towns on the coast as far as Seleucia. He kept plotting against Alexander,
and one day he sent a message to Demetrius the king, which said:
It was a big mistake to let Alexander marry her. He even tried to have me murdered!
Ptolemy said other insulting things about Alexander because he wanted his kingdom.
Then he ordered Cleopatra to leave Alexander, and he told Demetrius to marry her. Now Ptolemy and Alexander hated each other, and everyone knew it.
Ptolemy went to the city of Antioch, where he crowned himself king—both of Syria and of Egypt.
Meanwhile, Alexander had gone to the country of Cilicia because some towns there had rebelled against him.
When Alexander heard what Ptolemy had done, he attacked him, but Ptolemy's large army defeated Alexander and forced him to retreat.
After Ptolemy won this important victory, Alexander found a hiding place in Arabia,
but Zabdiel the Arab chopped off Alexander's head and sent it to Ptolemy.
Three days later, Ptolemy himself died, and the people in his fortresses killed the soldiers he had stationed there.
In the year 167 of the Syrian Kingdom, Demetrius the Second became king.
A little later, Jonathan gathered an army in Judea. He built a lot of weapons to break through city walls and then attacked the fortress in Jerusalem.
King Demetrius the Second found out about the attack from some Jews who really hated the other Jews.

Demetrius became furious, and right away he went to the city of Ptolemais. From there he wrote a letter to Jonathan and said, “Stop attacking the fortress in Jerusalem! Come to Ptolemais as soon as you can. We need to talk.”
After Jonathan read the letter, he ordered his soldiers to keep up the attack. Then he risked his own life by taking some of the priests and leaders
to Ptolemais. He brought silver, gold, some clothing, and many other gifts for Demetrius, which made Demetrius friendly toward him.
Some Jews who were unfaithful to their Law kept bringing charges against Jonathan.
But Demetrius treated him well, just as the rulers before him had done. And one day, when all the trusted friends of Demetrius were there, he gave Jonathan an even higher honor
by making him one of his most trusted friends. Demetrius also let Jonathan continue as high priest and keep all the honors he had already been given.
Jonathan asked Demetrius to stop collecting taxes from Judea and the three districts of Samaria, and, in return, he promised to give him 300,000 pieces of silver.
Demetrius agreed, then wrote the following letter:
King Demetrius sends greetings to his good friend Jonathan and to the Jewish nation.
I am sending you a copy of the letter I wrote about you to my friend Lasthenes, and here is what I said:
“King Demetrius sends greetings to his dear friend Lasthenes.
“The Jews are our friends, and I have decided to do them a big favor since they are loyal to us and can be trusted to keep their promises.
The three regions of Aphairema, Lydda, and Ramathaim, together with the land around them, used to belong to Samaria. Now they belong to Judea and are an official possession of the Jews.
And they don't have to pay me a tenth of their crops, the fee on salt, the special royal tax, or any other taxes.
“Lasthenes, no one may ever change even one of these orders.
Make a copy of this letter and send it to Jonathan. He will put it on God's holy mountain where it can be seen by everyone.”

No one opposed King Demetrius the Second, and his kingdom was at peace. So he sent his own soldiers back home and kept only the foreign troops he had hired from the Greek islands. But this made his own soldiers turn against him, because they had fought for many years, first in his father's army and then in his.

Trypho had been a follower of Alexander Epiphanes, and when he found out how angry all of Demetrius' troops were, he went to Imalkue the Arab, who was taking care of Antiochus the Sixth, the young son of King Alexander.

Trypho stayed with Imalkue a long time and kept begging him to hand over the young boy. He said, “Antiochus should take his father's place as king, because Demetrius has let all of his own soldiers go, and they hate him for it.”
Meanwhile, Jonathan sent the following message to Demetrius:
Demetrius wrote back:
For now, please do me a favor and send some troops to help me, because my own soldiers have rebelled.
Jonathan sent a heavily armed force of 3,000 soldiers to the city of Antioch, and Demetrius was very glad to see them.
Not long after this, a mob of about 120,000 people tried to kill Demetrius.
They took over the streets and started rioting. So Demetrius ran away to his palace
and ordered the Jewish soldiers to protect him.
They not only rescued Demetrius that day, but they also set the city on fire and took everything of value.
When the people of Antioch saw that the Jews had taken over their city, they were terrified and begged Demetrius for help. They shouted,
“Please make peace with us! Order the Jews to stop attacking us and our city.”

Demetrius made peace with the people as soon as they had put down their weapons. The Jewish soldiers had earned the respect of everyone in his kingdom, and they returned to Jerusalem with all the things they had captured.
Demetrius was now in complete control of his kingdom again, and there was no more trouble.
Before long, he forgot how much Jonathan had helped him, and he broke his promises to Jonathan by treating him like an enemy and causing him a lot of trouble.
When Trypho came back from his visit to Imalkue the Arab, he brought young Antiochus the Sixth with him, and the boy began to rule as king.
The soldiers that King Demetrius the Second had sent home now sided with Antiochus and Trypho. They attacked Demetrius, forcing him to run for his life.
Trypho captured Demetrius' elephants as well as the city of Antioch.
Young King Antiochus wrote a letter to Jonathan, in which he said:
I am sending you some gold plates and dishes, and I am giving you permission to drink from a gold cup and to wear royal robes and a gold buckle.
Your brother Simon is now the ruler of the land from Phoenicia to the Egyptian border.

Jonathan left Judea and led his army across the Jordan River. They were going from town to town, when the entire Syrian army arrived and offered to help them fight. So Jonathan took his forces to the town of Askalon, where the people welcomed and honored them.
He led his troops to the town of Gaza, but its people refused to let them enter. Then they surrounded the town and took everything of value from the villages nearby.
the people of Gaza begged him not to destroy their town. He agreed, but he sent the sons of Gaza's rulers as hostages to Jerusalem. After this, Jonathan led his army as far as Damascus.
Someone told Jonathan:
Simon stayed behind in Judea while his brother Jonathan set out to attack the army of Demetrius.
Simon attacked the town of Beth-Zur and kept it surrounded for a long time
before it surrendered to him. He took command of Beth-Zur and told its people to leave. Then he stationed his own troops there.
Meanwhile, Jonathan and his soldiers had set up camp near Lake Galilee. And early one morning, he led them to Hazor Valley.
Demetrius' army of foreign troops was waiting for them in the valleys. Some of them attacked immediately, while others waited behind some hills, ready to make a surprise attack.
When the enemy soldiers came out of their hiding places and attacked,
almost all the Jewish troops ran away, except two officers by the names of Mattathias and Judas.
Jonathan ripped his clothes and put dirt on his head to show his sorrow. Then he prayed
and returned to the battle. His army defeated their enemies and made them run for their lives.
When the Jewish troops that had deserted saw their enemies trying to escape, they returned and helped chase them as far as the enemy camp at Kadesh. The Jews set up camp there,
and Jonathan went back to Jerusalem. About 3,000 foreign soldiers were killed that day.
Jonathan realized this was a good time to make sure the Romans remained on friendly terms with the Jews. So he sent some messengers to Rome.
He also wrote letters to the city of Sparta and other places for the same reason.

When the messengers arrived in Rome, they met with the Roman senators and said, “Jonathan the high priest and the Jewish people have sent us here to renew our friendship with Rome and to make sure we remain allies.”
After the meeting, the Romans wrote letters to the other nations where the messengers were going. In these letters they said, “Help these men return safely to Judea.”
Jonathan himself wrote a letter to the people of Sparta in which he said:
Jonathan the high priest, the other priests, the Jewish council, and the rest of our people send greetings to our dear friends in Sparta.

Some time ago, your king, Arius, sent a letter to Onias, our high priest. Arius said that Jews and Spartans are related, as you can see from the copy of the king's letter we have sent along with this letter.
When Onias read this, he welcomed your messenger with honors, because your letter clearly stated that Jews and Spartans should become friends and allies.
We Jews don't really need friends and allies, since our Scriptures give us hope and strength.

But we decided to write you anyway to renew our friendship and to make sure that we are still on good terms. After all, it has been a long time since you wrote us, and we don't want to become like strangers to each other.
It is our custom and duty to remember relatives. So during our festivals and other special days, we always think of you as we pray and offer sacrifices.
We are very pleased that you have become so famous.
We have had plenty of troubles and wars of our own. Even the nearby kings have attacked us.
However, there was no reason to bother you or other friends and allies with our problems.
God always helps us, and we defeated our enemies and were rescued from them.
We have sent Numenius and Antipater as messengers to Rome to make sure that we and the Romans remain on good terms.
They also have orders to bring this letter to you with our greetings, because we want to be certain that you still consider us your relatives.
Please send a reply.
Here is a copy of the letter King Arius wrote to Onias some time ago:
“King Arius of Sparta sends greetings to Onias the high priest.
“We have found a document that says Spartans and Jews are relatives because both nations descended from Abraham.
Now that I know this, I want you to write and tell me how you are doing.
I am writing to tell you that your livestock together with everything else you own belongs to us. And our livestock together with everything else we own belongs to you.
Jonathan found out that the officers of King Demetrius the Second were now ready to invade his country with a more powerful army than before.
Jonathan did not want the king's army to invade Jerusalem, so he led his troops to the region around Hamath, where he saw the enemy camp.
Jonathan sent out spies, who came back and reported, “The king's army is getting ready to attack us tonight.”
At sunset, Jonathan stationed some of his troops on lookout duty around the camp, and he told the others, “Stay awake and be ready to fight at any time.”
But the king's troops lost their nerve and were frightened when someone informed them that the Jews were ready for their attack. So they lit campfires and ran away.
The campfires burned all night, and the Jews did not find out until morning that the enemy had left.
Jonathan sent troops after them, but the king's army had already crossed the Eleutherus River.
There was a tribe of Arabs named the Zabadeans, and Jonathan ordered his troops to destroy them. The troops took everything of value,
then Jonathan led them all the way to Damascus.
Jonathan returned to Jerusalem and met with the Jewish leaders. They decided to build fortresses in Judea

and to make Jerusalem's walls even higher. They also agreed to construct a strong, high wall between the enemy fortress and the rest of the city, in order to separate the fortress from the city and to keep enemy soldiers from going in and out for supplies.
Everyone worked together to rebuild Jerusalem; they repaired part of the collapsed eastern wall and the section of the city called Chaphenatha.
Meanwhile, Simon and his workers rebuilt the town of Adida at the edge of the hill country, and they put a wall around it with strong gates.
Trypho wanted to be king of Asia, and he began plotting against King Antiochus the Sixth.
But Trypho was afraid Jonathan would go to war to protect Antiochus. So he decided to do away with Jonathan, and he led his army to the town of Beth-Shan.
Jonathan and 40,000 of his best soldiers left Jerusalem to attack Trypho at Beth-Shan.
When Trypho saw the large army, he was too frightened to fight.
Instead, he brought Jonathan to his camp and gave him honors and gifts. Trypho bragged about Jonathan to all his trusted friends and troops and said, “Obey Jonathan's orders, just as you obey mine.”
Trypho told Jonathan:

I've come here to give you the city of Ptolemais and the other fortresses and to put you in charge of all the officers and troops. After I've done this, I'll go home. Choose a few troops to go with you and me to Ptolemais, then send the others back to Judea.
But as soon as he entered the city, its gates were closed. Then he was captured, and his soldiers were killed.
Trypho's troops and cavalry went to the Great Valley in Galilee to kill the rest of Jonathan's soldiers.
However, when Jonathan's troops heard what had happened to him and the others, they encouraged each other and marched away, ready to fight.
Trypho's soldiers and cavalry caught up with them, but they turned back when they realized that the Jews would fight for their lives.
After the Jewish soldiers from Galilee returned safely to Judea, the whole nation mourned for Jonathan and his troops. Everyone was terrified
because the Gentiles around there were saying, “The Jews have no ruler or general. Let's destroy them and make the world forget they ever lived.”
and encouraged everyone by saying:
and how they died fighting for our people.
But in these troubled times I'm ready to die for our people, just as my brothers did.
I want to get even with the other nations. They hate us and have come together to destroy our people, our temple, and our families.
Simon's speech encouraged everyone,
and they shouted, “Be our leader, just like your brothers Judas and Jonathan.
Take command of our army, and we will obey your orders.”
Simon called the troops together, and they worked quickly to finish the walls and towers that protected Jerusalem on every side.
Simon ordered Jonathan the son of Absalom to take a large force of soldiers to the town of Joppa. Jonathan forced the people to leave, and he took over Joppa.
Trypho was still holding Simon's brother Jonathan as a hostage, and he brought Jonathan along when he led his large army out of Ptolemais to invade Judea.
Your brother Jonathan was a royal official, but he owed money to the king, and so I arrested him.
I'll set him free as soon as you send me 100,000 pieces of silver and two of his sons as hostages. That way he won't rebel against me anymore.
Simon knew the messengers were lying, but he sent for the money and Jonathan's sons. He knew if he did not, the Jewish people would hate him and say,
“If Simon had given Trypho what he wanted, Jonathan would still be alive!”
Simon sent Jonathan's sons and the money to Trypho. However, Trypho broke his promise and did not release Jonathan.

Trypho and his soldiers now set out to invade and destroy the country. They marched south and came up on the road from Adora. But each time Trypho tried to cross the border, he was blocked by Simon and his forces.
Meanwhile, the enemy troops in the fortress at Jerusalem kept sending messages to Trypho, begging him to go around by way of the desert and bring them food.
Finally, Trypho ordered his cavalry to get ready to leave for Jerusalem.
When he reached the town of Baskama, he had Jonathan killed and buried.
Then he returned to his own country.
Simon had the body of his brother Jonathan taken back to Modein, the town of his ancestors. He buried him there,
and everyone in Israel cried and mourned for a long time.
Simon had a tall stone monument built over his family grave. It was shiny on the front and back, and could be seen a long way off.
He also built a row of seven pyramids to honor his father, his mother, and his four brothers.
Antiochus the Sixth was still a young boy when Trypho had him murdered.
Now Trypho was ruler and made everyone miserable.
During this time, Simon ordered the Jews to build thick walls, high towers, and strong gates for the fortresses in Judea and to supply them with plenty of food.
Simon sent messengers to King Demetrius the Second, and they begged him, “Please make things easier for our country. Trypho is robbing us of everything.”
Demetrius the Second did what Simon wanted and wrote him the following letter:
King Demetrius sends greetings to the Jewish people and their leaders, including Simon, who is high priest and a trusted friend of the king.
Thank you for the gold crown and the gold palm branch you sent me. I am ready to make a lasting peace by ordering my officials to stop collecting taxes from you.
I will give you everything I have promised in our treaties. Besides that, you can keep the fortresses you have just built.
I forgive everything you have done wrong in the past. And from now on, I won't collect the special royal tax or any of the other taxes I used to receive from Jerusalem.
I will hire any of your people who are prepared to help me in my kingdom. Let's give peace a chance!
So in the year 170 of the Syrian Kingdom, the Jews won their freedom from the Gentiles.
And on their documents and contracts they wrote, “The first year of Simon, the great high priest and the commander and ruler of the Jews.”

About this time, Simon and the Jewish forces surrounded the town of Gazara and set up a large weapon to break through the wall. They pushed it up to the town wall, where they broke through and captured one of the towers.
Then the soldiers who were operating the weapon rushed into Gazara, causing a terrible uproar.
Everyone in Gazara tore their clothes to show their sorrow. They climbed to the top of the town wall where they shouted to Simon and begged him for peace,
saying, “We've done wrong and deserve to be punished. But please have mercy on us.”

Simon agreed to stop the fighting. But he ordered everyone to leave the town, and he took the idols out of the houses where they were kept. Then he and his troops entered Gazara, singing hymns of praise.
Simon removed everything that made the town unclean according to their religion, and he made the fortresses of Gazara stronger. He built a house for himself and let faithful Jews live in the town.
The enemy troops in the Jerusalem fortress still could not go into the country to buy food, and many of them starved to death.
Finally, the survivors begged Simon for peace. He agreed, then ordered them to leave the fortress, so he could remove everything that made it unclean according to their religion.

On the twenty-third day of the second month in the year 171 of the Syrian Kingdom, Simon led his soldiers into the fortress. They carried palm branches and praised God with all kinds of songs and musical instruments. God had completely crushed their powerful enemy!

Simon decided that a joyous festival should be held on this same day every year. He strengthened the wall on the side of the temple hill that faced the fortress. Then he and his troops made the fortress their headquarters.
John the son of Simon was now a grown man. So Simon put him in command of the whole army, and John lived in the town of Gazara.
In the year 172 of the Syrian Kingdom, King Demetrius the Second led an army to the country of Media, where he hoped to hire soldiers to help him fight Trypho.
When King Arsaces of Persia and Media learned that Demetrius had invaded his country, he sent one of his generals
to capture him alive. This general defeated the army of Demetrius and took Demetrius to King Arsaces, who put him in prison.
The country was at peace
Simon became a true hero
Simon made the country larger
He took many prisoners
Life was peaceful on the farms;
In towns the old folks
Simon supplied the towns
He brought peace
Everyone rested unafraid
troublemakers and enemy kings
Simon helped the poor
He gave gifts to the temple
Cities as far away as Rome and Sparta mourned at the news of Jonathan's death.
But they were pleased that Jonathan's brother Simon had taken his place as high priest and ruler of Judea.
The Romans and Spartans wanted Simon to be their friend and ally, just as his brothers had been, so they wrote him letters on sheets of bronze.
The Jews then read these letters during a meeting in Jerusalem.
The letter from the Spartans said:
Your messengers made us very happy when they told us how famous you are.
The details of their visit are in our record books, which say:

We Spartans gladly welcomed these men and honored them. Moreover, we placed a copy of their message in the public building where all our record books are kept. We have also sent a copy to Simon the high priest, telling what we have done.”

After the Jews had finished their meeting, Simon sent Numenius to Rome to make certain that the Romans were still their allies. Numenius took them a heavy gold shield that weighed almost 570 kilograms.
When the people found out what Simon was doing, they said, “How can we repay Simon and his descendants?
He and his brothers and the rest of his father's family have been strong; they have defeated our enemies and set us free.”

“Simon the son of Mattathias was a priest from Joarib's family. He and his brothers risked their lives and fought back whenever our enemies attacked us. They protected our temple and the Law of Moses, and they made us famous.
“Simon's brother Jonathan united our people, and we chose him to be our high priest. But after he died,
our enemies prepared to invade Judea, because they wanted to attack our temple and destroy the country.
“Simon took command of our army. He spent a lot of his own money to pay our soldiers and to buy weapons and armor for us.
He put up strong walls and towers in the towns of Judea, as well as in the border town of Beth-Zur, where the enemy used to store weapons. Then he stationed Jewish soldiers at Beth-Zur.

“Simon built a fortress in the coastal town of Joppa as well as in the town of Gazara, because it was close to Azotus, which had been a stronghold for our enemies. Simon settled Jews in Gazara, and he gave everyone in these towns whatever they needed to make the towns fit to live in.
“Simon was a dependable man who had high hopes for our country and did all he could to make our nation glorious. So we chose him to be our ruler and high priest.

“The Gentiles had built a fortress in Jerusalem and had stationed some soldiers there, who then attacked the rest of us and made the temple and everything else unclean. But Simon successfully forced the Gentiles out of Judea; he got rid of the troops in the fortress and was in full control of everything.
“Simon strengthened the walls of the Jerusalem fortress and stationed soldiers there to guard the country and city. He also made the walls around Jerusalem higher.
“Simon did everything well, so King Demetrius accepted him as our high priest.
Demetrius called Simon his trusted friend and gave him many other honors.
He did this because he knew that the Romans had welcomed Simon's messengers and considered Jews their friends, allies, and relatives.
“Our people and priests gladly chose Simon and his descendants to be our rulers and high priests forever, or until God sends a true prophet.
“Simon will rule over us and care for our temple, our country, our weapons, and our fortresses.
Everyone must obey his orders and write his name on all official documents in Judea. Simon has permission to wear purple clothes and gold jewelry, just like a king.

“Our people and our priests must never change any of these orders. They must obey Simon and never hold meetings in the country without first asking him. And none of them may wear purple clothes and a gold buckle, as though they were kings.
Anyone who disobeys or rejects these orders will be punished.”
The agreement was written on sheets of bronze, then put in the temple for everyone to see.
Copies were also stored in the treasury for Simon and his family.
Antiochus the Seventh, the son of Demetrius the Second, sent a letter from the Greek islands to the Jews and to Simon the high priest and ruler.
It said:
Some rebels have taken control of my ancestors' kingdom. I want it back so I can make it a great kingdom again. I have hired a large army and navy,
and I am ready to land on the coast. I am going to punish everyone who has destroyed my country and ruined so many of its towns.
I will follow the example of other kings and excuse you from paying some taxes and fees.
I will let you make your own coins
and allow you to keep all of the weapons and fortresses you have built. As of today, I will remove all soldiers from Jerusalem and its temple,
and you won't be required to repay money you owe the king.
As soon as I get my kingdom back, I will make you and your temple prosperous and famous. Then the whole world will know how outstanding you are.

In the year 174 of the Syrian Kingdom, Antiochus the Seventh invaded the land of his ancestors. Soon most of Trypho's soldiers deserted and joined the army of Antiochus, leaving Trypho with only a few soldiers.
He retreated to the town of Dor on the coast, and Antiochus got ready to attack him there.
Trypho was in real trouble now, because he did not have enough troops to fight back.
Antiochus led 120,000 soldiers and eight thousand cavalry to Dor
and surrounded the town. At the same time, his ships attacked from the sea, and the people of Dor were trapped.
Meanwhile, Numenius and the other messengers returned to Jerusalem from Rome with letters to different countries and rulers. One of the letters said:
Lucius, a Roman official, sends greetings to King Ptolemy of Egypt.
Simon the high priest and the Jewish people have sent messengers to Rome to make sure that Jews and Romans are still friends and allies.
These messengers brought us a gold shield that weighs almost 570 kilograms.
If troublemakers escape from their country and come to you, they must be sent back to Simon the high priest, who will punish them according to the Law of Moses.
Lucius sent the same letter to King Demetrius and to Attalus, Ariarathes, and Arsaces.

It went to every country, including Sampsames and Sparta. And it went to Caria, Pamphylia, and Lycia, as well as to the islands of Delos, Samos, Rhodes, Cos, Aradus, and Cyprus and to the cities of Myndos, Sicyon, Halicarnassus, Cnidus, Gortyna, Cyrene, Phaselis, and Side.
Simon the high priest also received a copy of the letter.
Antiochus the Seventh made a second attack against the town of Dor. His soldiers set up weapons for breaking through the wall; they fought long and hard and kept Trypho from leaving.
Simon wanted to help Antiochus. So he sent him 2,000 of his best soldiers, together with silver and gold and many supplies.
Antiochus not only refused Simon's help, but he turned against him and broke every promise he had ever made.
Antiochus told his trusted friend Athenobius to meet with Simon and tell him:
along with others you have taken, belong to me, the king.
Simon, give back these towns and return the tax money from the places you captured outside of Judea.
If you don't want to do this, then pay 500,000 pieces of silver for damaging the towns you captured. And turn over to me 500,000 more to make up for the tax money you took from the towns.

When Athenobius arrived in Jerusalem, he could not take his eyes off Simon's great wealth. Simon had a table with dishes made of gold and silver, and he owned many other valuable things. Then Athenobius told Simon what the king had said.
Simon answered:
We intend to keep our land and property now that we have them back once again.
Meanwhile, Trypho had escaped by ship from Dor and sailed to the town of Orthosia.
Cendebeus led his army to Jamnia and started causing trouble in the town. He invaded Judea and killed everyone he captured.
After he made the fortress at Kedron stronger, he stationed some soldiers and cavalry there. Then he told them, “The king has ordered us to patrol the roads in Judea.”
Simon's son John went from Gazara at the time and told his father what Cendebeus had done.
Then Simon met with John and Judas, his two oldest sons, and said to them:
I am an old man now. But God has shown kindness by letting you become mature enough to lead our people in battle, just as my brothers and I have done. I pray that God will be with you as you fight!
John immediately left to attack Cendebeus with 20,000 foot soldiers and cavalry from Judea. That night, the troops made camp at Modein.
Then early the next morning, they went out to the valley and stopped beside a flooding stream. On the other side of it, a large number of soldiers and cavalry were moving toward them.
John lined up his troops for battle. He waded into the stream first, because he knew his soldiers were afraid of the water. They watched John, then followed him across.
John noticed that Cendebeus had a lot of cavalry. So John divided his men into groups and ordered them to take up positions around their own cavalry.
Then they blew war trumpets and attacked Cendebeus. His forces ran away, and many of his troops died in the battle. Those who escaped ran back into their fortress.
During the battle, John's brother Judas was wounded. But John and his troops chased the enemy soldiers. Some of them ran as far as Kedron, the town that Cendebeus had rebuilt.
Others reached the towers in the open country near the town of Azotus. But John burned the town and killed about 2,000 enemy troops. After this, he led his army safely back to Judea.
Ptolemy the son of Abubus was in command of the valley near Jericho. He was a rich man
and was married to the daughter of Simon the high priest.
But Ptolemy was very proud and thought he deserved to be the ruler. So he began plotting to kill Simon and his sons.

In the year 177 of the Syrian Kingdom, Simon was going from town to town in Judea, trying to help the people. Later that year during the month of Shebat, he and his sons Mattathias and Judas arrived in Jericho.
Ptolemy pretended he was glad to see Simon and his sons. Then he invited them to a banquet in their honor at a small fortress that he had built and named Dok.
As soon as Simon and his sons were drunk, the soldiers rushed out of their hiding places with swords in their hands. They attacked Simon, his two sons, and some of their servants, killing them all.
So Ptolemy betrayed a friend and proved that he could not be trusted.
Ptolemy wrote and told King Antiochus that he had killed Simon. He asked the king to give him soldiers and to put him in command of Judea and its towns.
But someone warned John, “Ptolemy has already murdered your father and brothers. And now he has sent soldiers to kill you!”
John was shocked by this news. He found out which soldiers had come to kill him, and he had them arrested and put to death.
The Jews of Jerusalem and Judea wrote a letter to their Jewish relatives in Egypt. It said:
We pray that God will be kind to you and remember the promise that he made to his faithful servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
May God make you willing and eager to worship and obey him with all your heart.
May he bless you with peace and with an understanding of his Law and its commands.
We ask him to answer your prayers and forgive your sins and never turn from you in times of trouble.
All of us here are now praying for you.
In the year 169 of the Syrian kingdom, when Demetrius was our ruler, we wrote you a letter in which we said:

They destroyed the temple gate and killed innocent people. But we begged the Lord for help, and when he answered our prayers, we brought sacrifices and offerings of grain into the temple. We lit the lamps and put the sacred loaves of bread on the table.”
And so, we now urge you to celebrate in the month of Chislev a festival like the Festival of Shelters.
The Jews of Jerusalem and Judea had also written an earlier letter. It said:
We thank God because he has rescued us from King Antiochus, who put us in dreadful danger.
The king's troops attacked our holy city of Jerusalem, but God forced him to retreat.
They set out the treasures, and when Antiochus and a few of his friends entered the temple, the priests immediately locked the doors behind him.

Then they killed him and his friends by dropping heavy stones on them from a trap door in the roof. Afterwards, the priests chopped the dead bodies into pieces and tossed the heads to the people outside.
Let's always praise our God for punishing these wicked enemies!

On the twenty-fifth day of the month of Chislev, we will celebrate the Temple Festival. We think you need to know this, so you can celebrate it just as you celebrate the Festival of Shelters and the Festival of Fire.

All this happened long ago, when our ancestors were dragged away to Persia, and some faithful priests took fire from the altar. They secretly hid the fire at the bottom of a dry cistern, and they hid it so well that no one ever found it.

Many years later, when it pleased God, the Persian king sent Nehemiah back to Jerusalem. Nehemiah then told some descendants of those priests to find the hidden fire. But after returning, they told us, “There is nothing in the cistern except an oily liquid.”
Then, after the sacrifice was ready, Nehemiah ordered the priests to sprinkle the liquid over the offerings and the firewood,
and they did. A little while later, the sun came out from behind the clouds. Then the firewood and offerings suddenly burst into flames, as everyone stared in amazement.
While the offerings were being burned, a priest named Jonathan began praying. Nehemiah, the other priests, and the rest of the people also joined in the prayer
that went something like this:
No one else is fair and gives us everything we need; no one else is all-powerful and lives forever.
“Please accept our sacrifice that we are offering for everyone in Israel, your chosen nation. Protect us from danger and make us holy.
“Bring home our scattered people and free those Jews who are slaves in foreign nations. We are hated and mistreated. So have pity on us and show Gentiles that you are the God of Israel.
“Take revenge against our arrogant enemies, who attack and insult us.
Then give your nation a lasting home in your holy land, just as Moses said you would.”
When everyone had finished praying, the priests started singing hymns.
Soon the fire burned up the offerings. Then Nehemiah ordered the rest of the liquid to be poured over some large rocks.
As soon as this was done, the rocks started burning, but flames from the altar put out the fire.

People everywhere heard what had happened. Even the Persian king learned that an oily liquid had been discovered in the place where the priests had hidden the altar fire just before they were dragged away to Persia. The king was also told that Nehemiah and his followers had offered a sacrifice, using the liquid to start their fire.
After the king had carefully checked on this story, he surrounded the cistern with a high wall and built a shrine there.
Then the king exchanged gifts with the people he liked.
Nehemiah and his followers called the oil “nephthar,” which means “cleaning.” But everyone else calls it “naphtha.”
One of our writings says that it was Jeremiah the prophet who ordered our people to hide some of the altar fire before we were forced to go to Persia, just as I have already told you.

We also know from this writing that Jeremiah taught these Jews the Law of the Lord. He warned them never to forget the Lord's commands after they arrived in Persia, and he also begged our people not to be tricked into worshiping idols, even the ones decorated with gold and silver.
He said many similar things, while urging them to always think about the teachings of the Law.

This same writing tells us that Jeremiah had a vision, in which he was ordered to take the sacred tent and the sacred chest to the mountain that Moses had climbed to look at the land God had promised us.
After Jeremiah came to the mountain, he found a big cave, where he hid the tent, the chest, and the altar for burning incense. Then he blocked the entrance to the cave.
Meanwhile, a few of our people had followed Jeremiah, hoping to mark the path to the cave, but they could not.
Jeremiah got angry with them when he discovered what they had tried to do, and he said:

At that time, he will show where these things are hidden. A cloud will appear, blazing with God's own dazzling light, just as it did when he came to Moses. This is also how the Lord came to King Solomon, when Solomon asked him to make the holy temple glorious and acceptable as a place for worship.”
We also know that Solomon was wise and built our temple, then offered a sacrifice to make it completely acceptable.
When Solomon prayed, some fire came down from heaven and burned up his sacrifices. This is the same thing that happened when Moses prayed,
“I am offering a sacrifice for sin. So it must be completely burned, and none of it eaten.”
Solomon's festival lasted for eight days.

You will find all this information in our record books as well as in the writings of Nehemiah, who built a library and filled it with the writings about prophets and kings. The books of King David and the letters that the kings wrote about offerings are also in his library.
Judas Maccabeus collected all the books we had lost track of during the war, and we still have them here.
Send someone after these books if you ever need them.
We are ready to celebrate the Temple Festival, and so we are writing to say that you should celebrate it as well.
God has rescued his nation and returned our sacred land that we inherited from our ancestors. God has also given us back our kingdom, our priests, and our sacred way of life,

just as he promised in the Law of Moses. He has saved us from dreadful danger and made our temple holy again. Because of this, we will always trust in the kindness of God, who will bring us back home from every nation on earth and lead us to his holy temple.
They are so full of facts and details that they discourage readers who want to learn about these events.
My shorter version will please everyone—people who read for pleasure will enjoy it, and those who like to memorize things will find it easy to remember.
My story is merely a summary of the main events included in Jason's account.
He was like a builder who had to know every detail about the new house he was constructing. I am simply a decorator whose only job is to make things look beautiful.
Historians learn as much as possible about their subjects, then present every side of a story, without leaving out a thing.
But writers who summarize books are allowed to be brief and to leave out many of the details.
Enough said is enough said! Now is the time to begin the story itself. How foolish it would be to write such a long introduction that I would have to leave out part of the history.
When Onias was high priest of the nation, the holy city of Jerusalem always had peace. Onias hated evil and loved God, which made everyone careful to obey the Law.
Many kings showed great respect for the temple in those days and even brought it expensive gifts.
For example, King Seleucus of Asia used to pay for the daily sacrifices with money from the taxes he collected.
While Onias was still high priest, a man named Simon from the Benjamin tribe was a high official in the temple. And one day he started arguing with Onias about how to run the Jerusalem marketplace.
Simon lost the argument and went to Apollonius, the governor of Southwest Syria Province,
and said, “There is more money in the temple treasury than can be counted. And since the money is not used to pay for sacrifices, it may as well be placed under the authority of the king.”
Apollonius told King Seleucus about the money in the temple, and the king ordered Heliodorus, his highest official, to bring it to him.
So Heliodorus left at once for Jerusalem. But he told everyone that he was on his way to inspect the towns of Southwest Syria Province.
Onias the high priest warmly welcomed Heliodorus to Jerusalem. Then Heliodorus explained, “I came to the city because someone told me there is a lot of money in your temple treasury. Is this true?”
Onias answered:
and some of it belongs to Hyrcanus, a very important man. At the most, you will find only 400,000 silver coins and 200,000 pieces of gold. That devil Simon lied to you.
Anyway, I can't possibly let you rob our people of their silver and gold. They trust this sacred temple and think their money is safe. After all, everyone in the world respects this holy place.
Heliodorus answered, “King Seleucus has ordered me to collect the money for the royal treasury, and I'm going to do just that.”
After Heliodorus had set a day to collect the money, he went into the temple to take charge of the workers who were counting the silver and gold.

The priests in their sacred robes were lying face down on the ground in front of the altar and praying, “Our God, please protect this silver and gold! You yourself made the law that keeps our money safe while it is stored in the temple.”
It was heartbreaking just to look at Onias the high priest. His face was pale because of his suffering,
and his trembling body showed that he was terrified and tormented.
Heliodorus was about to disgrace the temple, and so families ran out of their houses and huddled together in the streets to pray.
Grown women put on sackcloth skirts. Young women who had never been allowed outdoors ran to the city gates or to the city wall, or just stared out of their windows.
Everyone raised their hands toward heaven, begging God for help.
It was a dreadful sight to see the high priest in such anguish and agony and the people lying face down on the ground.
Everyone kept begging the Lord All-Powerful to protect the money that had been left in the temple.
In the vision, they saw a gruesome rider with gold weapons and gold armor. The rider's horse wore a fancy harness and charged furiously at Heliodorus, kicking at him with its hoofs.
Two very strong and handsome young men in fine clothes suddenly appeared. One stood on each side of Heliodorus and beat him severely with whips,
until he fainted and fell to the ground. Then his guards picked him up and placed him on a mat.
Only a short time before this happened, Heliodorus had led a crowd of followers and guards into the treasury. Now they had to carry this helpless man away, and everyone clearly saw the power of God.
After Heliodorus had seen and felt God's mighty strength, he lay speechless and near death.

But everyone else praised the Lord God All-Powerful because of the miracle that had kept the temple safe. A little while earlier, the temple was filled with fear and confusion, but now there was joy and happiness because the Lord had appeared.
Heliodorus was at the point of death, and a few of his friends quickly begged Onias to ask God Most High to let him live.
Onias did not want King Seleucus to think that the Jews had plotted to kill Heliodorus. And so he offered a sacrifice and asked God to make Heliodorus well.

While Onias was offering the sacrifice, the two young men appeared to Heliodorus again. They were still dressed in their fine clothes, and they said, “Heliodorus, you should be grateful for Onias! It was because of him that the Lord did not take your life.
God in heaven was the one who punished you. Now you must tell everyone how powerful God is.” After saying this, the young men disappeared.
Heliodorus offered his own sacrifice, then made a lot of promises to the Lord who had saved his life. He said goodbye to Onias and led his soldiers back to King Seleucus.
He told everyone, “With my own eyes, I have seen God Most High work miracles.”
One day, Seleucus asked Heliodorus, “Who should I send to Jerusalem this time?”
“Send someone you don't like or an enemy of your government! Whoever you send will be killed or badly beaten, because God's power surrounds the Jerusalem temple.
This God lives in heaven, but he guards that place and kills everyone who tries to harm it.”
So God kept Heliodorus from robbing the temple treasury.

I have already told you that Simon caused a lot of trouble for our country by telling Apollonius about the money in the temple. Then later, Simon lied and blamed Onias for the attack on Heliodorus and for all the terrible things that happened.

Simon even dared to claim that Onias was plotting against the government, although everyone knew that Onias had been generous to Jerusalem and that he had protected our nation and had been in favor of its laws.
Simon hated Onias so much that he had even hired some men to commit murders.
Apollonius, the governor of Southwest Syria Province, started encouraging Simon with his evil plans. Finally, Onias understood that his life was in danger,
and he asked King Seleucus for help. Onias did not want to bring charges against other Jews. He only hoped to find ways of privately and publicly doing good for the entire nation.
But he knew that he needed the king's help to bring peace to the country and to bring Simon to his senses.
After the death of King Seleucus, Antiochus Epiphanes became ruler. Shortly afterwards, Jason, the brother of Onias, became high priest by bribery.
Jason went to the king and promised him 360,000 silver coins from one of his accounts and 80,000 from another.

He also agreed to pay 150,000 silver coins for permission to do two things. He wanted to make the Jews in Jerusalem citizens of Antioch, and he wanted to build a place where young Jewish men could exercise and have organized sports.
King Antiochus gave Jason everything he wanted. But no sooner had Jason become high priest than he began forcing Jews to live like Greeks.
He did away with our rights that John, the father of Eupolemus, had received from former kings. Eupolemus was the messenger who later went to the Romans and made them our friends and allies.
He eagerly built the place for exercise and sports near the temple. Then he ordered our finest young men to take part in activities there.
Jason was so terribly evil that he did not deserve to be high priest. In fact, it was his fault that our people began to adopt the foreign customs that came with the Greek way of life.

Even our priests gave up worshiping at the altar. They cared nothing about the temple, and they neglected offering sacrifices. And when the signal was given, they hurried off to take part in games that were against our teachings.
They sneered at the values our ancestors had prized, and their only goal in life was to receive Greek honors.

This love of the Greek way of life caused the downfall of our country, when these foreign rulers became our enemies and punished our nation. They did this, even though many Jews liked and tried to follow their way of life.
When people disobey God's Law, they are taking a big risk, as the following events will show.
King Antiochus attended a sports festival that was held once every four years in the city of Tyre. While he was there,
that evil Jason sent some messengers from Jerusalem to Tyre with 300 silver coins for a sacrifice to the god Hercules.
to give the money for building warships.

About this same time, Antiochus sent Apollonius to Egypt, so that Apollonius could attend the crowning of King Philometor. When Antiochus learned that Philometor had become his enemy, he took actions to protect his kingdom. Then Antiochus left for Jerusalem, passing through the town of Joppa on the way.
In Jerusalem, Jason and a cheering crowd with torches gave him a glorious welcome. From Jerusalem, Antiochus led his army to Phoenicia.
Three years later, Jason sent a man by the name of Menelaus to King Antiochus with money in order to do some important business. Menelaus was the brother of the Simon who was mentioned earlier.

Menelaus was introduced to the king and tried to impress him by acting like a powerful official. Then he bought the position of high priest by offering the king 300,000 silver coins more than Jason had offered.

When Menelaus returned to Jerusalem, he carried papers from the king, saying he was the new high priest. But he was completely unfit for the job—he was cruel and had a violent temper worse than any wild animal.
Jason had earlier cheated his brother Onias out of the position of high priest. And now someone was cheating him out of being high priest, and he had to run to the Ammonites for his own safety.
Menelaus continued as high priest, though he never paid any of the money he had promised Antiochus.
He was asked many times for it by an official named Sostratus, who commanded the enemy fortress in Jerusalem, and whose duty it was to collect the king's money.
Menelaus let his brother Lysimachus act as high priest while he was away. Sostratus assigned his responsibilities to Crates, the commander of the soldiers from Cyprus.
About this time, King Antiochus gave the cities of Tarsus and Mallus to his lover Antiochis. But the cities rebelled,
and the king hurried off to put down the revolt, leaving a senior official named Andronicus in charge of the kingdom.

Menelaus now saw his chance to steal some gold dishes from the temple, and he did it. Then he gave the dishes to Andronicus. Earlier, he had also taken gold dishes from the temple and sold them to the people of Tyre and of other nearby cities.
Onias found out what had happened and ran for safety to a temple at Daphne, not far from the city of Antioch. There he started publicly accusing Menelaus.

Shortly after this, Menelaus met privately with Andronicus and persuaded him to kill Onias. So Andronicus went to the temple and warmly greeted Onias. Then he lied to Onias by shaking his right hand and promising to treat him with kindness. Onias didn't really trust Andronicus, but Andronicus talked him into leaving his place of safety in the temple. Then without any regard for the Law, Andronicus murdered him on the spot.
Our people were shocked and outraged by this violent murder, and so were many from other nations.
When King Antiochus returned from Cilicia, the Jews in Antioch asked him to do something about this senseless crime. Many Greeks also told the king how much they despised this brutal murder.
The king cried and grieved terribly as he thought about Onias, a man of common sense and self-control.

Then he became furious and tore off Andronicus' clothes, including his royal robe. He made Andronicus walk naked through the whole city until they reached the place where Andronicus had murdered Onias. Right then and there, the king had this butcher put to death.

In the meantime, Menelaus had been helping his brother Lysimachus rob the Jerusalem temple of its gold dishes and other sacred objects. News of these crimes spread, and a crowd got together to complain about Lysimachus.

But since this crowd was turning into an angry mob, Lysimachus handed out swords to about three thousand followers. He put a foolish old man named Auranus in command of this force, then ordered a brutal attack.
Our people saw Lysimachus and his troops running toward them. So they immediately picked up rocks, as well as handfuls of ashes and chunks of wood. They threw them wildly at the attackers,
wounding many and killing a few, while the rest ran away. The temple robber Lysimachus was killed not far from the temple treasury.
Because of what had happened, Menelaus was charged with serious crimes
and put on trial in the city of Tyre when King Antiochus arrived there. The Jerusalem council sent three messengers, who testified against him.
When Menelaus realized he was going to be punished, he offered a huge bribe to the king's friend Ptolemy, because he wanted Ptolemy to influence the king to say he was innocent.
So Ptolemy took Antiochus out on a porch, saying they needed a breath of fresh air. He convinced Antiochus to change his mind
and to drop the charges against Menelaus, the cause of the trouble.
but Antiochus had them quickly and wrongfully killed. He did this because they had spoken in behalf of Jerusalem, its people, and the sacred dishes that had been stolen.
The citizens of Tyre were so disgusted by the murder of these three men that they honored them with elaborate funerals.
But because our rulers were greedy, Menelaus was allowed to continue as high priest. He grew so cruel that we considered him our worst enemy.
About this time, King Antiochus began a second invasion of Egypt.
And for more than 40 days, the people of Jerusalem saw visions of cavalry in gold armor, galloping through the air. The cavalry rode in companies, and the riders were holding spears and swords.

They lined up like armies facing one another, then they attacked and counterattacked. Gold ornaments and all kinds of armor glittered and sparkled in the sunlight. Shields flashed, and spears and arrows filled the sky.
Everyone prayed that these visions meant something good.

Soon a rumor spread around that King Antiochus was dead. Right away, Jason got together a force of over 1,000 soldiers and made a surprise attack on Jerusalem, defeating the troops that Menelaus had stationed on the city walls. After this, they captured the city and forced Menelaus to retreat to the fortress overlooking the temple.

But Jason kept on killing more Jews, without realizing that a victory which destroys your own people is the worst possible defeat. He seemed to think he had won a battle against enemies rather than against other Jews.
But Jason wasn't able to take control of the government. In fact, he was so disgraced by what he had done that he had to run for his life once again to the country of the Ammonites.
Afterwards, he died a miserable death.
then sailed to Sparta,
Because he didn't even bury
When King Antiochus heard about the fighting in Jerusalem, he thought that Judea had rebelled against him. So in his fury, he led his army from Egypt and captured Jerusalem.
Then he ordered his soldiers to kill everyone they found, even those hiding in their own homes.
As though that were not enough, Antiochus walked straight into the world's most sacred temple and was shown around by Menelaus, who had betrayed our laws and our nation.
Then, with his own filthy hands, Antiochus took away sacred dishes and helped himself to the treasures given by other kings to the honor and glory of the temple.

Antiochus was really proud of himself. But he did not understand that the Lord was punishing the people of Jerusalem, because they had sinned and made him angry for a while. And this was the reason the Lord had let Antiochus disgrace the temple.

If the people had not sinned so terribly, the Lord would have beaten him with whips and stopped him from doing such a foolish thing, just as he did to Heliodorus, when Seleucus sent him to examine the treasury.
But the Lord did not choose the nation for the good of the temple. He chose the temple for the good of the nation.

That's why the temple and our people suffered together and were later blessed together. So when God All-Powerful got angry with us, he deserted our temple. But after God had made peace with us, he gave the temple back its glory.
After King Antiochus had stolen 1,800,000 silver coins from the temple, he rushed back to Antioch, arrogant and drunk with power. He believed he could walk on water and sail on dry land!
